transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Good afternoon, Mrs Achterberg. I'm Dr Sandhu, one of the cardiology registrars. And you've come with...?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My daughter, Rosalind.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Hello.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Lovely. I've got the letter from your GP. You were diagnosed with atrial fibrillation about eighteen months ago, is that right?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, about then.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How have you been getting on?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've been more puffed out lately, going up the stairs. And I can feel my heart fluttering.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long has that been going on?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Three weeks, perhaps a little more.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any chest pain?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, no pain.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any dizziness or blackouts?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit light-headed once or twice when I stood up quickly, but I haven't fainted.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do your ankles swell?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A little, by the evening.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Can you lie flat at night?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, one pillow, same as always.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Now, you're on a blood thinner, apixaban. How are you taking that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Once a day, in the morning.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: No, Mum, it's twice. Morning and night. I fill your dosette box every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, is it? Yes, she does the box. Twice then.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you, that's important. Five milligrams each time?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Yes, five milligrams.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any bleeding problems? Nosebleeds, bruising, blood in your water or your stools?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Well, there was some blood when I went to the toilet, three weeks ago. Fresh red blood. Just the once.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Mum, you never told me that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I didn't want to make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'm glad you told me. Has it happened again since, or any black stools?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, just the once.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any change in your bowel habit, or weight loss?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And what else do you take?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The bisoprolol, two and a half milligrams. And my thyroid tablet, levothyroxine, 75 micrograms.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Codeine makes me sick.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, intolerance to codeine. Let me examine you. Your pulse is irregularly irregular at about 104 a minute. Blood pressure is 128 over 76. Let me listen to your heart. Irregular, and no murmur that I can hear. Your chest has a few crackles right at the bases on both sides. Mild swelling around both ankles. Your weight today is 58 kilos.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've lost a bit.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Your bloods from last week: your kidney function is reduced, with a creatinine of 140, and your thyroid level is normal too. The ECG today shows atrial fibrillation with a rate of about 105.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: So what does that mean?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It means your heart rate is still a bit fast, which is likely why you're more breathless. I'd like to increase the bisoprolol from two and a half to five milligrams once a day.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: All right.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd also like an echocardiogram, a scan of the heart, within the next six weeks, to check how well it's pumping, given the crackles and the swelling.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Your apixaban dose of two and a half milligrams twice a day is correct for you, because of your weight and kidney function, so we'll keep that the same. But the bleeding you mentioned needs looking into. I'll ask your GP to do a blood count and arrange a FIT test, the stool test, and consider a referral to the bowel team.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Should she stop the blood thinner?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: No. Please don't stop it. Stopping it would put her at risk of a stroke. One episode isn't a reason to stop, but we do need to find the cause.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If you have any more bleeding, especially a lot of blood, black stools, or you feel faint, go to A&E. And if your breathing gets much worse, especially lying flat, or you get chest pain, call 999.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Got it.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll see you back in clinic in three months, after the echo.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you, doctor.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Increased exertional breathlessness and palpitations for 3 weeks, on a background of atrial fibrillation diagnosed 18 months ago.
reference_note.history: Breathless on stairs, palpitations. No chest pain. Occasional postural light-headedness; no syncope. Mild evening ankle swelling. No orthopnoea. Single episode of fresh red rectal bleeding three weeks ago, not previously reported; no recurrence, no melaena, no change in bowel habit or weight loss. Attended with daughter, who manages her dosette box.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (initially reported as once daily; daughter confirmed twice daily). Bisoprolol 2.5 mg once daily. Levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. Codeine intolerance (nausea).
reference_note.examination: Pulse irregularly irregular, rate 104. BP 128/76. Heart sounds irregular, no murmur. Fine bibasal crackles. Mild bilateral ankle oedema. Weight 58 kg. ECG: atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate approximately 105. Bloods: creatinine 140, thyroid function normal.
reference_note.impression: Atrial fibrillation with suboptimal rate control, likely contributing to breathlessness; possible early heart failure. Reduced renal function (creatinine 140). Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily appropriate (two dose-reduction criteria: weight 58 kg, creatinine 140). Single episode of rectal bleeding on anticoagulation requiring investigation.
reference_note.plan: Increase bisoprolol to 5 mg once daily. Echocardiogram within 6 weeks. Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily; do not stop. Letter to GP: FBC, FIT, and consider lower GI referral. Clinic review in 3 months after echocardiogram.
reference_note.safety_netting: Attend A&E if further significant bleeding, black stools or feeling faint. Call 999 if breathing worsens significantly, especially lying flat, or chest pain.
